data.name: Vishrut
data.gender_notes: Vishrut is used as a unisex name in Hindu naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Derived from the Sanskrit word 'Vishruti', meaning 'truthful' or 'honest'. The name Vishrut carries the meaning “Truthful, Honest” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit, Hindi, etc. tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Vishrut usually hope their child will grow to embody truthful, honest and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: Symbolizes integrity, authenticity, and respect for truth.
data.etymology: Vishrut belongs to the Sanskrit, Hindi, etc. linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Truthful, Honest.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Vishrut total 9, giving a life-path number of 9. Number 9 is linked with Mars and with the qualities of compassion, idealism and generosity.

data.cultural_impact: The name Vishrut is considered a noble and respected name in Hindu culture, reflecting values of truthfulness and honesty which are highly revered in Hindu society. It is believed that individuals with this name possess strong moral character and high integrity.
data.spiritual_significance: In Hinduism, truth and honesty are key virtues leading towards spiritual growth and enlightenment. The name Vishrut reminds one of the importance of living a truthful life in alignment with dharma (duty) and artha (prosperity). It is believed that the energy of this name supports one in staying true to their inner path and values, enabling deeper spiritual connection and self-realization.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Vishrut: The one who has attained the supreme truth and wisdom, a wise and virtuous soul.

vedic_reference.note: Vishrut is a popular name in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism.

historical_references.reference: Vishrut was a famous Jaina scholar and monk during the 2nd century BCE in India. He is best known for his work 'Tattvartha Sutra' which is a fundamental text in Jaina philosophy.

Another reference to Vishrut can be found in the 'Ashoka's Rock Edict No. 1'. Ashoka, the great Mauryan Emperor of India, mentions Vishrut as one of the four teachers of Dharma who were sent to preach his edicts throughout the empire.
